 WASHINGTON (TNND) — On Capitol Hill this week, a tense Senate hearing about the precarious future of Social Security illustrated just how far lawmakers are from passing reforms to prevent its looming insolvency.
 On Capitol Hill this week, a tense Senate hearing about the precarious future of Social Security illustrated just how far lawmakers are from passing reforms to prevent its looming insolvency. (TNND) 
 Democrats and Republicans agree the program is in trouble. They also agree they need to act quickly . What that action should look like is the source of an ongoing partisan clash preventing current and future beneficiaries from having confidence that the system they paid into will be there for them when they retire.
 In short, more money is going out than coming into the Social Security trust fund. According to the latest report by the Trustees of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, if nothing changes, Social Security beneficiaries will see at least 22% across-the-board cuts by 2032. That timeline could be moved up as persistent inflation swells annual cost-of-living adjustments.
 Congress has been aware of the lopsided payment-to-collection ratio for decades, but lawmakers repeatedly punted the issue to future leaders. Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., let his frustration about this show during an interview before Wednesday’s hearing on the issue.
 At this point, there’s really no way to fix Social Security. It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and you hope that you can recover some of your money,” Johnson said on Fox Business. Democratic committee members accused him of resorting to scare tactics.
 "We're going to need people to stop freaking posturing on their favorite cable show and actually come to the table with solutions,” Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said.
 Johnson later cleaned up his comments, acknowledging his word choice was meant to draw attention to the problem.
 I realize I’m making myself a lightning rod here. The only way people were going to watch this hearing is if we talked about it as a legal Ponzi scheme. We’ve had hearing after hearing, no one pays attention. Maybe now the American people will pay attention. If I’ve got to pay a political price for that, that’s fine. I really don’t care. I’d rather go home,” Johnson said. Johnson argued Congress should pass a bill to prevent benefit cuts and then tackle the “big problem” of the trust fund’s shortfall.
 Potential fixes include raising the retirement age – a politically toxic move with scant support – or reducing benefits for the highest earners. There are also various ways to generate more revenue by taxing investment income like capital gains or, the option with the most bipartisan traction, raise the cap on taxable income. Currently, payroll income above $184,500 is not taxed for Social Security .
 “For the wealthiest Americans, most of their income comes from investments. Some earn no wages at all,” Senate Budget Committee Ranking Member Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said. “They simply borrow against the assets so they never pay into the Social Security fund. They should support the trust fund like every other worker.”
